activities.caption: file the stall's costs — fixed or variable
activities.name: ueCostBuckets

config.prompt: Fixed costs are the price of existing; variable costs scale with each unit. File them:

items.label: the loan payment on the tea urn

config.why: The split matters because the two lines behave differently: one ignores volume, the other rides on it — and the gap between them is where profit lives.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the break-even arithmetic
activities.name: ueBreakevenCloze

config.text: Each cup contributes £4 − £2.50 = %%0%% toward the fixed costs. With rent of %%1%% a month, break-even is 240 ÷ 1.50 = %%2%% cups — the sales you must make before the business earns anything at all.
config.hint: Contribution first, then divide the rent by it.

activities.anchor: One more number matters in practice
activities.caption: call the cushion — margin of safety
activities.name: ueSafetyEstimate

config.prompt: Selling 240 units against a 160-unit break-even — how big is the margin of safety, as a percentage of sales?
config.why: About 33 per cent: an 80-unit cushion. A 15 per cent dip in demand survives it; a 40 per cent dip does not.
config.context: Every cup after number 160 drops £1.50 of profit straight to the bottom.

activities.anchor: The widget's defaults are the same stall
activities.caption: run the experiments — move a line, take the consequence
activities.name: ueExperimentBranch

config.root: The big stall: price £40, variable cost £25, fixed costs £2,400 — break-even 160 units. Move one line and watch the consequence.

start.text: The bank wants a lower break-even. Which line do you move?

choices.label: Raise the price
choices.feedback: The crossing slides left — fewer sales needed. But will customers stay?

choices.label: Cut the variable cost per unit
choices.feedback: The gap between the lines widens — every unit after break-even earns that gap as profit.

choices.label: Double the fixed costs to grow faster
choices.feedback: The whole cost line rises: break-even moves right, and the business lives or dies on volume.

price.text: Higher margin per unit — the classic high-fixed-cost dilemma: fewer sales needed, more lost if demand sags.

variable.text: Cheaper tea leaves, in effect — contribution up with no new risk of demand.

fixed.text: This is why airlines, chip factories and cinema chains live or die on volume.

config.why: Profit is not a line on the chart — it is the vertical gap between the two lines, and every experiment moves one of them.

activities.caption: pair each production method with its trade-off
activities.name: ueMethodMatch

config.prompt: Three methods of production — pair each with what it buys:

pairs.right: maximal customisation, high cost per unit, no economies of scale

pairs.left: batch production (a bakery's rye then sourdough)
pairs.right: some variety and some scale — but every switch costs setup time
lowest unit cost, but inflexible, and a line stoppage is expensive

config.why: Services run the same spectrum: a bespoke consultancy is job production; a coffee chain is flow production with milk.

activities.caption: one line of the lean summary is wrong
activities.name: ueLeanSpot

config.prompt: One line of this lean-production summary is wrong. Find it.
lines: Lean production's target is every form of waste — the Japanese word is muda
Just-in-time holds days of parts, not months, freeing cash and warehouse space
The cost is vulnerability to supply shocks, as the pandemic showed
Kaizen means big redesigns proposed by outside consultants twice a year
Error-proofing means defects never restart a process
config.correction: Kaizen means continuous small improvements proposed by the people doing the work.
config.why: Lean's insight is accounting disguised as philosophy: inventory is money sitting still, and time is a cost line.

activities.anchor: actual output as a percentage of maximum output
activities.caption: drop the marker on the factory's utilisation
activities.name: ueUtilisationPlace

config.prompt: A factory pays full fixed costs while earning revenue on only part of its capacity — it runs at what utilisation in the example? Place the marker:
config.why: 60 per cent: high utilisation is how the fixed-cost line gets spread — which is why airlines discount last-minute seats rather than fly them empty.

activities.anchor: They are fixed only with respect to output
activities.caption: true or false — the word 'fixed' on trial
activities.name: ueFixedJudge

statements.s: Rent does not care whether you sell 10 cups or 1,000 this month.
statements.why: Fixed versus variable describes how a cost behaves when volume changes — nothing more.

statements.s: Fixed costs are fixed forever — the landlord can never raise them.
statements.why: The landlord can raise the rent next year; 'fixed' means fixed with respect to output.

statements.s: A big restaurant chain's locations each repeat the same small-scale costs, so being huge brings no scale economies automatically.
statements.why: Ask which cost line moved, not how big the firm is.

statements.s: A small firm can enjoy purchasing economies by joining a buying cooperative.
statements.why: Scale economies come from spreading fixed costs and buying inputs cheaper — both visible without size.
